ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Prior to data collection, we received ethics approval from our university's institutional review board to run this study.

We used a combined word-picture verification and difference recognition task paradigm in which participants were required to choose which of two presented chemical structures matched the presented chemical name.
Informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Participants filled out a brief questionnaire that asked them to report their current role (faculty, post-doctoral fellow, graduate student, undergraduate student, or staff member), area of study (chemistry, biology, physics, etc.), and undergraduate chemistry courses taken, if the participant was an undergraduate student.

Based on the information collected in the questionnaire, we could not classify participants who were either staff members or undergraduate students who have not taken any chemistry courses at our university into these groups.
These participants are represented in Group 4.
Participants completed a series of 36 randomized trials in which they viewed a pair of organic molecules and an IUPAC name (Figure 2).
table.formatted: Participants completed a series of 36 randomized trials in which they viewed a pair of organic molecules and an IUPAC name (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

table.text: For each trial, participants had a maximum of 15 seconds to select which organic molecule matched the IUPAC name.
In word-picture verification tasks, participants are presented with an image and word (e.g., an image of a fish and the word "fish") and must decide if they match.

N* 1 Chemistry faculty, post-doctoral fellows, and graduate students 27 2 Undergraduate students who have already taken second-year organic chemistry 34 3 Undergraduate students who are currently taking first-year chemistry or second-year organic chemistry 42 4 Other (staff members, undergraduate students that have not taken chemistry courses) 29 *After exclusion of participants due to poor eye-tracker calibration or high data loss.
Each participant completed each of these 36 trials.
Participants were seated 60-65 cm away from the monitor in a dim room.
Participants had smaller Hs,s on trials with cyclic targets (M = 0.564, SD = 0.178) than acyclic targets (M = 0.589, SD = 0.159).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .01", "p < .05", "p < .05"), 
    Text = c("Trial accuracy was very weakly negatively correlated with Hs,s, ρ(4750)= -.168, p < .001, and Hs,n, ρ(4750)= -.046, p < .01.", 
    "Participants in Groups A and B generally exhibited smaller Hs,s than Groups C and D, which was significant by pairwise t-tests (p < .05).", 
    "All pairwise t-tests among complexity conditions were also significant for Hs,n (p < .05)."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

In word-picture verification tasks, participants are presented with an image and word (e.g., an image of a fish and the word "fish") and must decide if they match.

text.text: Chemists use verbal and visual representations of molecules to communicate and solve problems, yet little is known about how chemists efficiently interpret them simultaneously with ease.
Participants (N = 200) of varied chemistry expertise completed an experiment in which they solved short representation-matching tasks with bond-line structures and IUPAC names of organic molecules.

Drawing upon information-processing theory and prior chemistry education research on representational processing efficiency, we examined how expertise and varied task characteristics affected visual scanning efficiency.
We recorded participants' eye movements during the tasks to quantify the extent to which their gaze was focused or exploratory using a metric called stationary gaze entropy.

Chemistry experts exhibited more focused gaze within the bondline structures presented, which suggests that they more efficiently apply more chunk stimuli and activate prior knowledge connecting the representations.

By looking at the effects of varied structural features and complexity, we outline inadvertent challenges that chemistry novices may face while processing these representations during chemistry instruction.
We offer chemistry instructors suggestions for mitigating demands on their students' working memory.

We also propose avenues for follow-up research that will allow chemistry instructors to better understand how to scaffold their students' development of the implicit skills associated with chemistry expertise.

Chemists regularly use multiple representations, like bond-line structures and disciplinary vocabulary, to communicate and reason about phenomena that are unobservable to the naked eye. 1, 2 These representations are often likened to a foreign language. [3] [4] [5] In organic chemistry, bond-line diagrams of molecules are used ubiquitously to communicate the structure and reactivity of molecules.

text.text: In their study, students spent more attention on provided ball-and-stick representations compared to electrostatic potential when students were provided different prompts like determining the site of nucleophilic attack in the molecule. 74 Few chemistry education research studies have explicitly examined the efficiency of information-processing of chemical representations, though. 22 Disciplinary experts have several perceptual advantages in their processing of discipline-specific stimuli. 29, 36, 75, 76 Foundational eye-tracking research was done by psycholinguists to outline the perceptual advantages and eye movement patterns of skilled readers. 58, [77] [78] [79] Countless research articles in this discipline have used eye movements to study the information-processing underlying word recognition, sentence comprehension, and reading passages, 78, [80] [81] [82] which have built the basis for the eye-mind hypothesis. 58 Two examples of these advantages, as discovered by research on reading, are: (i) With more experience viewing a type of stimulus, readers or other disciplinary experts develop a wider perceptual span, which describes the area at which they can peripherally encode information on a stimulus from a single fixation. 75, 78, 83 (ii) Fluency in a language is associated with efficient retrieval of semantic representations between words and their picture referents, which manifests as faster fixations toward matching pictures in specific experimental paradigms. 84, 85 In terms of informationprocessing theory, advantage (i) relates to the encoding of stimuli in working memory, and advantage (ii) relates to the retrieval of multimodal semantic representations from long-term memory and their effects on visual attention.

text.text: We argue that the visual processing of bond-line structures of organic molecules may come with similar expertise advantages.
In this study, we examined stationary gaze entropy (Hs) for capturing the spatial allocation of attention to visual diagrams of molecules, which are two-dimensional and modular.

Stationary gaze entropy quantifies the extent to which gaze is dispersed across areas of a stimulus, 44, 64 and was chosen because it aligned with established theory, precedent, and our context. 86 Stationary gaze entropy has been used extensively to study the processing efficiency of complex visual environments and how visual attention is affected by top-down and bottom-up processes. 44 For goal-driven tasks, stationary gaze entropy is negatively correlated with top-down gaze control. 44 That is, the more focused one's gaze is on a stimulus, the more they are affected by top-down processes due to repeated exposure to the same type of stimulus.

text.text: Our study addresses the following research questions:
To what extent do features of the stimuli and/or multimodal cue affect the dispersion of visual attention during this task, and how do these effects differ between experts and novices?

text.text: 4 Chemistry experts' repeated exposure to chemical diagrams and names may facilitate chunking of these disciplinary stimuli in working memory.

Analogous to the increased perceptual span of experienced readers, 75, 78, 83 we expect this effect to manifest as less dispersed viewing on representations in tasks that require one to encode a chemical diagram or name.

text.text: Via chunking, experts could encode the entire representation in working memory with fewer distinct fixations.
This is expected to be influenced by various features of the stimuli including complexity, aspects of the chemical structure, or differences between the presented structures.
Similarly, the retrieval of long-term semantic knowledge may be efficient enough to directly affect visual attention.

This retrieval has been observed to occur implicitly during name-picture matching tasks. 84, 85 Hence, we expect chemistry experts to focus their attention on relevant portions of each representation in a task in which they must match a bond-line structure and IUPAC name.

Prior to data collection, we received ethics approval from our university's institutional review board to run this study.
Recruitment and data collection occurred at a Canadian national chemistry conference and at our university.
We set up a data collection booth at which potential participants could review the study details and decide whether to take part.
Our booth was located at high foot traffic spots at both sites.
Conference attendees and university students, faculty, and staff (N = 200) volunteered to participate in the study.
Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
Participation in the study took 5-10 minutes, and we did not provide compensation to participants.

Participants filled out a brief questionnaire that asked them to report their current role (faculty, post-doctoral fellow, graduate student, undergraduate student, or staff member), area of study (chemistry, biology, physics, etc.), and undergraduate chemistry courses taken, if the participant was an undergraduate student.
We used participants' answers to this questionnaire to assign them one of four groups of expertise (Table 1).

text.text: We use these groups to roughly model participants' experience processing chemistry representations.

Group 1 contains participants with the most experience (chemistry faculty, post-doctoral fellows, and graduate students), and Group 3 contains participants with the least experience (undergraduate students currently in first-or second-year chemistry courses).

Based on the information collected in the questionnaire, we could not classify participants who were either staff members or undergraduate students who have not taken any chemistry courses at our university into these groups.
These participants are represented in Group 4.
We did not collect any other demographic information like ethnicity or gender because they are not the focus of our research questions, and we wanted to minimize risks of data reidentification.

text.text: For each trial, participants had a maximum of 15 seconds to select which organic molecule matched the IUPAC name.
A fixation cross was displayed for 500 ms to center participants' gaze prior to each trial.
The task used in our experiment is a blend of two experimental paradigms from cognitive psychology: word-picture verification tasks and difference recognition tasks.
In word-picture verification tasks, participants are presented with an image and word (e.g., an image of a fish and the word "fish") and must decide if they match.

This paradigm is used to study how semantic representations are activated from long-term memory during multimodal processing. [95] [96] [97] [98] In difference recognition tasks, participants must locate the difference between a pair of images.

text.text: Target type has two conditions referring to whether the target is cyclic or acyclic.
Complexity has three conditions based on the number of carbon atoms and functionalities in the target.
Finally, foil type has six conditions based on the visually salient difference between the target and foil.

For instance, in stimuli in the extra group condition, the foil contains a functionality that is not present in the IUPAC name, and in stimuli in the missing group condition, the foil is missing a functionality that is present in the IUPAC name.
Our 2×3×6 factorial design allowed 36 unique combinations of task characteristic conditions.

Each participant completed each of these 36 trials.

Eye movements during the experiment were recorded with a Tobii Pro Spectrum 300 eye-tracker.
This device is attached to a 23.8" monitor with a resolution of 1920 x 1080 pixels.
Participants were seated 60-65 cm away from the monitor in a dim room.
The eye-tracker was calibrated for each participant using a nine-point calibration procedure.
The position of the participant's gaze on the monitor is recorded by the eye-tracker at a sampling rate of 300 Hz.
The Tobii Pro Velocity- pg.
6 Threshold Identification Gaze Filter was used to preprocess the eye-tracking data.
This algorithm classifies eye movements as fixations or saccades if movements in gaze position are slower or faster than 30 °/s, respectively.
Visual angle degrees (°) are calculated based on the distance of the participant from the monitor and the monitor's size.
Gaze position measurements from the left and right eye were averaged during data preprocessing.

Data was excluded from our analysis for participants with poor calibration accuracy (above 0.5°) and participants who had at least one trial with high data loss (above 20%). 99 The final sample included in our analysis contained 132 participants.

text.text: The maximum value of Hs is standardized to 1, allowing for its comparison across trials with different values of 𝑠.
We calculated two separate stationary gaze entropy metrics: one for the structures in the stimuli (Hs,s) and one for the names in the stimuli (Hs,n).
The areas of interest that are used in the stationary gaze entropy calculation were defined systematically for each stimulus.
For the molecular structures, we followed a protocol recently developed by Langner and colleagues that algorithmically defines areas of interest around each atom in a molecule.
Using this method avoids the bias of manual definition of areas of interest on findings.

As recommended by the authors, we set the radius of each area of interest equal to the bond length in the structural diagrams. 101 An example definition of structure areas of interest for a stimulus is shown in Figure 3(a).

text.text: Using an experiment that prompted participants to choose the bond-line structure that matched a provided IUPAC name, we investigated how top-down processes like visual chunking and multimodal cueing affected gaze behavior on each type of representation.

We used stationary gaze entropy, a metric calculated from the eye movements we captured during the experiment, to examine how participants' experience in chemistry and varied characteristics of the tasks modified the role of these top-down processes.
To answer our first research question, we compared the stationary gaze entropy of participants based on their self-reported chemistry expertise.

To answer our second research question, we varied the characteristics of the trials based on whether molecules were cyclic or acyclic (target type), the size of the molecules (complexity), and the type of visually salient difference between the two molecules (foil type).
We found that participants with more chemistry expertise generally exhibited more focused attention within the bond-line structures.

While our analysis does not reveal whether these participants focused on more relevant portions of the stimuli, they generally sampled less information across the bond-line structures, which is associated with top-down gaze control. 44 Based on prior research, it is likely that experts focus their attention towards task-relevant features of disciplinary stimuli. 36, 66, 69 Most of the information in the bond-line structures is redundant, and experts have been found to ignore provided information that is not useful for solving chemistry tasks. 64 We found that accuracy per trial was only weakly correlated with focused gaze behavior, which suggests that sense-making skills and representational processing efficiency play distinct roles in the tasks. 22, 23 That is, being able to accurately match bond-line structures with IUPAC names does not necessarily mean one completes the task efficiently.

text.text: By contrast, we found no evidence that the extent to which attention was dispersed across components of the IUPAC names differed for experts and novices.

The intrinsic segmentation of morphemes in the IUPAC names (either phonetically or visually with dashes) may allow for domain-general chunking via bottom-up means. 82, 104, 105 Even though the name is read with our eyes, the encoding of the IUPAC names occurs verbally in the phonological loop, 106, 107 which may not affect gaze behavior in the same way as visual chunking.

text.text: Further, compared to the atoms of the bond-line structures, attention was generally more evenly distributed across components of the IUPAC names.
This may be because the name is generally read left-to-right, whereas there is no constrained sequence for scanning the bond-line structures.
Participants may need to sample the entire name in this manner before comparing it to the bond-line structures.
It is also possible that this experiment cannot elicit topdown effects on the visual scanning of IUPAC names.
Our target type conditions isolated the observed effects to top-down effects of visual chunking.
This is because the content and task demand of the IUPAC names between these trial types only differed in the presence of cyclo for the cyclic targets.
As such, we suggest that any effects due to cueing from the IUPAC name should be the same across cyclic and acyclic target types.
We found that gaze across atoms in the structures was more focused during cyclic trials, but upon further investigation, we only observed this effect for participants with higher expertise.

Contrary to our hypotheses that bottom-up facilitation of chunking would occur similarly for all participants due to Gestalt principles like grouping, [46] [47] [48] this suggests that these features of cyclic molecules may not govern experts' more focused attention within the cyclic molecules.

text.text: This also contrasts work by Stieff and colleagues that investigated chemistry novices' encoding of ball-and-stick models in a change detection task.

They found that novice chemists leveraged spatial groupings in the stimuli during encoding that corresponded to expert chunks. 40 We considered that novice participants may always engage in the exploratory scanning associated with dispersed gaze behavior, 44 which could be due to uncertainty during the task and lack of sense-making skills.

text.text: These participants' visual scanning was sensitive to the other manipulations of task characteristics, though, so we argue that students may face inadvertent challenges working with visual representations containing cyclic molecules.

Chemistry instructors may overlook this challenge while highlighting structural information in a cyclic molecule or asking their students to copy down a mechanism containing cyclic molecules, both of which require the student to encode the visual in working memory.

We found that regardless of expertise, participants exhibited highly dispersed viewing behavior across the bond-line structures for trials in which the visually salient cue was the misplacement of a parent functional group or substituent.
We had anticipated that experts may have experience counting carbon atoms on organic molecules and would still exhibit more focused viewing relative to novices.
This skill may hence not be a component of their representational processing efficiency, perhaps due to limited repeated exposure to this type of task.

It is also possible that counting does not demand much of visual working memory, as chunking strategies are typically employed implicitly to lessen load working memory during difference recognition tasks. 28

text.text: The visually salient difference between structures was generated in the same way for each complexity level.
For each trial, increasing stimulus complexity made structures longer or introduced additional functionalities that were common to both structures presented.
As such, the added information is redundant and not directly relevant for distinguishing the structures based on the IUPAC name.
The observed effect may hence be due to exploratory viewing resulting from poor cueing from the IUPAC name.

As the name becomes longer, the cue distinguishing the correct and incorrect structure becomes less apparent, which doesn't allow for multimodal cueing to filter attention towards specific structural features.
Our variation of the foil type modified the type of visually salient difference between the structures and the corresponding cue in the IUPAC name that distinguished them.
Because the type of difference could have marked effects on its recognition, 29 pg. 12 we compared trials in which the incorrect structure either had an extra group or was missing a group.

text.text: We found that participants exhibited more exploratory viewing substantially more for the former condition, which we argue is due to the lack of a direct cue in the IUPAC name (i.e., there is nothing in the IUPAC name for this condition indicating that the group is not meant to be there).

We also found that viewing was generally exploratory across trials of all complexity for this condition, which suggests that without the presence of the cue buried in the name, the main effect of complexity is less dramatic.

By contrast to our observations for attention on the bond-line structures, participants attended to components of the IUPAC names more evenly for low complexity stimuli compared to medium or high complexity stimuli.

Because this also contrasts the related research on visual scene complexity, 87, 88 we suggest that attention allocation on the names may be affected by different processes than that of the structures.

As the names became longer, though, participants may have implicitly began to skim or chunk multiple components together to avoid cognitive overload. 28 The effects of varied foil types on attention allocation within the IUPAC names were like the effects described for the bondline structures.

text.text: The way that the cue in the name is delivered (as varied by foil type) may hence also affect visual attention within the name.
If a participant is searching for clues to help with their solving of the task, and does not find one (e.g., in the extra group condition), they may continue viewing the name exploratively.
We frame these implications in terms of some of the inadvertent challenges that students may face while processing multiple modes of representations during chemistry instruction.
Foremost, our findings suggest that chemistry novices are inefficient in their encoding visual representations and translating between verbal and visual representations of organic molecules.

Perceptual learning activities embedded in course designs could address this issue, 23, [110] [111] [112] [113] and analogous activities for organic nomenclature may be adapted from previous work. text.text: We also revealed that chemistry novices may encounter difficulties viewing cyclic molecules, even though they feature domain-general spatial grouping.

Because the chemistry experts in our study exhibited visual-cognitive advantages over novices while viewing cyclic molecules, this challenge to learners may be especially easy for chemistry instructors to overlook.
Instructors should aim to be conscious of how much time is provided for students to view and/or write down visual representations during instruction or assessment.

That the relevant information in increasingly complex stimuli is difficult for both novices and experts to discern supports the practice of introducing representation types gradually while explicitly explaining their purposes and connections. 35 Further, effective signaling strategies (i.e., signaling students' attention to specific features of representations during instruction) used with complex representations may similarly help students build representational processing efficiency. 99, 114, 115 Implications for Research Our work builds upon research that has investigated how attention is allocated to visual representations during chemistry problem solving and the importance of representational processing efficiency in chemistry learning. text.text: Chemistry experts more efficiently processed information during the tasks, and our analysis showed the various ways in which visual chunking and multimodal cueing allowed for these informationprocessing advantages.

Building off of this work and a report of chemistry novices' ability to use expert chunks without having chemistry expertise, 40 we suggest that future research explore how the morphology of bond-line structures may make them easier or harder to chunk by chemistry novices (i.e., via bottom-up processes).

text.text: We note several limitations of the present study.
Our interpretations of eye movements are limited by the design of our experiment, which explored how chunking and multimodal cueing affected gaze behavior.
Because our experiment combined a difference recognition task and a word-picture matching task, we cannot isolate the effects of either of these processes.
We use our task variations to better interpret each effect independently, but we note that further experimentation is needed to more confirm our findings independently from one another.

We did not collect a standardized measurement of sense-making skills in IUPAC naming, so we could not characterize the complex interplay between representational sense-making skills and processing efficiency.
We use participants' self-reported expertise to represent their exposure to chemical structures and names (not their sense-making skills).
Another limitation of our study is that our interpretations of eye movement data are not cross validated with other sources of data.

Retrospective think-alouds can reveal participants' problem-solving strategies during experiments in which eye movements are recorded, 109 which may have allowed us to confirm that participants' viewing strategies were affected by working memory capacity and/or multimodal cueing.

text.text: This study explored how chemistry expertise and varied task characteristics influence the processing of visual and verbal chemistry representations.
We captured chemistry experts and novices' eye movements while they solved a series of representation-matching tasks involving bond-line structures and IUPAC names of organic molecules.
Within each type of representation, we used these eye movements to calculate participants' stationary gaze entropy, which indicates to what extent their attention was dispersed.

We found that chemistry experts exhibited focused viewing among atoms of the bond-line structures, which we attributed to the top-down effects on gaze from their repeated exposure to chemistry representations.

Repeated exposure is likely to allow chemistry experts to chunk components of the stimuli more efficiently in working memory and more efficiently retrieve semantic representations relating the verbal and visual representations. 21, 39, 85 We discerned between these top-down effects by varying the characteristics of the task, such as whether the molecules were cyclic and how complex the molecules were.

text.text: Our findings suggest that disciplinary chunking may be especially efficient for cyclic molecules.

For some types of trials, expertise had much weaker effects on visual attention, which allowed us to generate potential boundaries for how chemistry experts' representational processing efficiency interacted with the tasks.
We also found that conditions in which the relevant cue in the IUPAC name were less explicit were associated with more dispersed visual attention.
For instance, participants generally exhibited higher stationary gaze entropy for stimuli containing longer IUPAC names (higher complexity).
For these stimuli, the relevant cue is surrounded by more information that does not directly help one solve the task.
Thus, the degree to which multimodal cueing affects gaze behavior may be modulated by the accessibility of the cue.
Chemistry experts and novices both exhibited relatively exploratory viewing among portions of the IUPAC names.
This indicates that top-down processing may affect attention towards visual and verbal representations in distinct ways.

Whereas attention within bond-line structures became more exploratory as their size increased, attention within the IUPAC names became more focused for longer names, which may reflect changing scanning strategies or chunking employed to mitigate demands on working memory.

Taken together, these findings extend research on representational competence in chemistry education by highlighting the role of representational processing efficiency in processing multiple modes of representations simultaneously.
Our analysis reveals the advantages that chemistry experts have during processing and inadvertent challenges that varied task demands may pose to chemistry novices (and occasionally experts).
We hope that our work provides a foundation for future research and instructional interventions aimed at building chemistry students' representational competence.
